items.meaning: A polite, understated way to comment on good weather, often used to start a conversation.
items.example: It's quite pleasant out today, isn't it? Much better than yesterday.
items.plain: The weather is nice today, isn't it? Much better than yesterday.
items.note: A common, gentle opener for small talk, suitable for any casual setting.

items.meaning: Used to politely introduce an observation about someone or something nearby, often as a conversation starter.
items.example: I couldn't help but notice your interesting book; is it a new release?
items.plain: I saw your interesting book and wanted to ask if it's a new release.
items.note: A polite way to comment on something without seeming intrusive. Can be used with 'that' or a noun phrase.

items.meaning: A common, polite way to ask someone why they are at a particular place or event.
items.example: So, what brings you here to the conference this year?
items.plain: Why are you at the conference this year?
items.note: Standard and friendly. Avoids being too direct like 'Why are you here?'

items.text: I hope you don't mind me asking
items.form: I hope you don't mind me asking
items.meaning: A polite preface to a potentially personal or slightly intrusive question.
items.example: I hope you don't mind me asking, but how long have you been working in this field?
items.plain: May I ask how long you've been working in this field?
items.note: Shows consideration for the other person's privacy. Use for slightly sensitive topics.

items.meaning: A polite way to initiate an introduction when you suspect you haven't been introduced before.
items.example: We haven't met, have we? I'm Sarah from the marketing team.
items.plain: I don't think we've met before. I'm Sarah from the marketing team.
items.note: Common in professional or semi-formal social settings. Invites an introduction.

items.meaning: Expressed when you discover an unexpected connection or coincidence with someone.
items.example: You know John from university? Small world, isn't it! He was my flatmate.
items.plain: You know John from university? That's a coincidence! He was my flatmate.
items.note: A friendly, informal expression to acknowledge a surprising shared connection.

items.meaning: A gentle way to introduce a question or a suggestion, making it sound less demanding.
items.example: I was just wondering if you'd tried the new coffee shop downstairs.
items.plain: Have you tried the new coffee shop downstairs?
items.note: Softens the inquiry, making it more conversational and less like an interrogation.

items.meaning: Used to make a polite observation about someone's current activity or state, often to open a conversation.
items.example: It looks like you're enjoying the exhibition; which piece is your favourite?
items.plain: You seem to be enjoying the exhibition; which piece is your favourite?
items.note: A non-intrusive way to comment on someone's actions or appearance, inviting a response.

items.meaning: A common and polite question to ask if someone is having a good time at an event or activity.
items.example: Are you enjoying the conference so far? I found the morning session quite insightful.
items.plain: Is the conference good so far? I found the morning session quite insightful.
items.note: A standard, friendly question for social or professional gatherings.

items.text: I'm afraid I didn't catch your name
items.form: I'm afraid I didn't catch your name
items.meaning: A polite way to ask someone to repeat their name if you missed it during an introduction.
items.example: I'm afraid I didn't catch your name earlier; could you remind me?
items.plain: Could you please tell me your name again? I missed it.
items.note: More formal and polite than 'What's your name again?' Shows good manners.

items.meaning: A polite way to acknowledge and show appreciation for someone's contribution to a discussion.
items.example: That's an interesting point about the market trends; I hadn't considered it from that angle.
items.plain: Your idea about the market trends is good; I hadn't considered it from that angle.
items.note: A versatile phrase for showing engagement and respect in a conversation.

items.meaning: Used to indicate that you understand someone's perspective or argument.
items.example: I see what you mean about the project timeline; it does seem ambitious.
items.plain: I understand your point about the project timeline; it does seem ambitious.
items.note: A common and natural way to show comprehension and empathy.

items.meaning: A phrase used to introduce a frank or slightly critical opinion, softening its impact.
items.example: If I'm being honest, I found the presentation a little dry.
items.plain: To be frank, I found the presentation a little dry.
items.note: Adds a touch of sincerity and can make a critical comment sound less harsh.

items.meaning: Used to introduce a contrasting idea or a different perspective in a discussion.
items.example: The new policy has its benefits, but on the other hand, it might create more bureaucracy.
items.plain: The new policy has its benefits, but it might also create more bureaucracy.
items.note: Helps to present a balanced view or introduce a counter-argument politely.

items.meaning: A mild expression of agreement, often indicating slight reluctance or uncertainty.
items.example: Do you think we should reschedule? I suppose so, if everyone else is busy.
items.plain: Do you think we should reschedule? Yes, probably, if everyone else is busy.
items.note: Conveys agreement without strong enthusiasm, or a concession. Very common in British English.

items.meaning: A polite way to express mild disagreement or to qualify someone's strong statement.
items.example: He's a genius, but I wouldn't go that far; he's certainly very capable.
items.plain: He's a genius, but I don't agree with that strong statement; he's certainly very capable.
items.note: A diplomatic way to temper an opinion without directly contradicting someone.

items.meaning: A polite way to express uncertainty or to hedge a statement, avoiding a definitive answer.
items.example: I'm not entirely sure when the report is due, but I can check for you.
items.plain: I don't know exactly when the report is due, but I can check for you.
items.note: Useful for hedging and showing politeness, especially when you don't have full information.

items.meaning: A polite and open-ended way to ask for someone's opinion on a particular topic.
items.example: What are your thoughts on the new hybrid working model?
items.plain: What do you think about the new hybrid working model?
items.note: Encourages a more detailed response than a simple 'Do you like it?'

items.meaning: Used to smoothly transition to a new topic or share a related anecdote.
items.example: That reminds me of a similar situation we had with a client last year.
items.plain: That makes me think of a similar situation we had with a client last year.
items.note: A natural way to shift the conversation or introduce a personal story.

items.meaning: A polite and engaging way to express interest in learning more about something.
items.example: I'm curious to know how you got into your line of work.
items.plain: I'd like to know how you got into your line of work.
items.note: Shows genuine interest and encourages the other person to share more.

items.meaning: Used to express empathy and shared experience with what someone else is saying.
items.example: You're feeling overwhelmed by deadlines? I can relate to that completely.
items.plain: You're feeling overwhelmed by deadlines? I understand that feeling completely.
items.note: A warm and connecting phrase that builds rapport in conversation.

items.meaning: Used to introduce a reasonable or generally accepted statement, often as a summary.
items.example: It's fair to say that the project exceeded expectations.
items.plain: We can reasonably conclude that the project exceeded expectations.
items.note: Adds a sense of objectivity and reasonableness to a statement.

items.meaning: A slightly formal but polite way to express agreement, often with a hint of consideration.
items.example: Given the new data, I'm inclined to agree with your assessment.
items.plain: Given the new data, I tend to agree with your assessment.
items.note: More formal than 'I agree,' suggesting a thoughtful consideration of the point.

items.meaning: A polite and diplomatic way to express doubt or disagreement without being confrontational.
items.example: I'm not convinced that this approach will solve the underlying issue.
items.plain: I doubt this approach will solve the underlying issue.
items.note: Softens disagreement, focusing on your own perspective rather than directly challenging theirs.

items.meaning: Used to introduce an important point or consideration that should not be forgotten.
items.example: It's worth bearing in mind that the budget is quite tight this quarter.
items.plain: Remember that the budget is quite tight this quarter.
items.note: A gentle way to remind someone of a fact or introduce a new, relevant piece of information.

items.text: I'm just trying to get a sense of
items.form: I'm just trying to get a sense of
items.meaning: Used to explain that you are attempting to understand the general nature or feeling of something.
items.example: I'm just trying to get a sense of the team's overall mood regarding the changes.
items.plain: I'm trying to understand the team's overall mood regarding the changes.
items.note: A common, polite way to explain why you're asking questions or observing.

items.meaning: Used to correct a widely held but incorrect belief in a polite and informative way.
items.example: It's a common misconception that all organic food is healthier.
items.plain: Many people wrongly believe that all organic food is healthier.
items.note: Allows you to correct information without making the other person feel foolish.

items.meaning: A polite way to indicate that you don't understand what someone is saying and need clarification.
items.example: I'm not sure I follow your logic on that last point; could you elaborate?
items.plain: I don't understand your logic on that last point; could you explain more?
items.note: More polite than 'I don't understand,' as it implies the fault might be yours.

items.meaning: Used to rephrase something for clarity or to offer a different perspective.
items.example: To put it another way, we need to prioritize efficiency over speed.
items.plain: In other words, we need to prioritize efficiency over speed.
items.note: Helpful for ensuring understanding or for simplifying a complex idea.

items.text: I'm afraid I don't quite agree
items.form: I'm afraid I don't quite agree
items.meaning: A very polite and softened way to express disagreement.
items.example: I'm afraid I don't quite agree with your interpretation of the data.
items.plain: I don't fully agree with your interpretation of the data.
items.note: Highly diplomatic and formal, suitable for professional or sensitive discussions.

items.meaning: Used to describe a situation where two things are very similar but distinct, and one can easily cross into the other.
items.example: It's a fine line between being assertive and being aggressive in negotiations.
items.plain: There's a subtle difference between being assertive and being aggressive in negotiations.
items.note: Highlights nuance and complexity, showing sophisticated understanding.

items.meaning: Used to indicate that you are arguing a point you may not believe in, to stimulate discussion.
items.example: I'm just playing devil's advocate, but what if we considered the worst-case scenario?
items.plain: I'm just arguing the opposite side for discussion, but what if we considered the worst-case scenario?
items.note: A useful phrase for exploring ideas thoroughly without committing to a position.

items.meaning: A genuine and polite admission that someone has presented a new and valid perspective.
items.example: You're right, I hadn't thought of that potential consequence.
items.plain: You're right, I didn't consider that potential consequence.
items.note: Shows openness to new ideas and respect for the other person's input.

items.meaning: Used to indicate that you are undecided about something and haven't made a choice yet.
items.example: I'm still on the fence about whether to take the new role or stay where I am.
items.plain: I haven't decided yet whether to take the new role or stay where I am.
items.note: A common, informal idiom for expressing indecision.

items.meaning: Used to suggest that it's too soon to draw conclusions or make definitive judgments about something.
items.example: We've only just started the project, so it's early days yet to predict its success.
items.plain: We've only just started the project, so it's too soon to predict its success.
items.note: A common, understated British English phrase for 'it's too soon to tell'.

items.text: I'm just trying to wrap my head around
items.form: I'm just trying to wrap my head around
items.meaning: Used to explain that you are trying to understand something complex or difficult.
items.example: I'm just trying to wrap my head around the new tax regulations.
items.plain: I'm trying to understand the new tax regulations.
items.note: A common, slightly informal idiom for grappling with a complex idea.

items.text: I'm not sure where I stand
items.form: I'm not sure where I stand
items.meaning: Used to express uncertainty about your opinion or position on a particular issue.
items.example: On the issue of remote work, I'm not sure where I stand yet.
items.plain: On the issue of remote work, I haven't formed a clear opinion yet.
items.note: A common, honest way to express indecision or a lack of a firm opinion.

items.text: I'm just trying to get a handle on
items.form: I'm just trying to get a handle on
items.meaning: Used to explain that you are trying to understand or manage a situation or topic.
items.example: I'm just trying to get a handle on all the new responsibilities in my role.
items.plain: I'm trying to understand and manage all the new responsibilities in my role.
items.note: A common idiom for gaining control or understanding of something complex.

items.meaning: Used to explain that you are attempting to assess or estimate something.
items.example: I'm just trying to gauge the level of interest in the upcoming workshop.
items.plain: I'm trying to assess the level of interest in the upcoming workshop.
items.note: A polite way to explain why you're asking questions or observing reactions.

items.text: I'm just trying to make sense of
items.form: I'm just trying to make sense of
items.meaning: Used to explain that you are attempting to understand something confusing or illogical.
items.example: I'm just trying to make sense of all the conflicting information.
items.plain: I'm trying to understand all the conflicting information.
items.note: A common, empathetic way to describe grappling with confusing data.

items.text: I'm just trying to get a feel for
items.form: I'm just trying to get a feel for
items.meaning: Used to explain that you are attempting to understand the general atmosphere or character of something.
items.example: I'm just trying to get a feel for the company culture before I decide.
items.plain: I'm trying to understand the company culture before I decide.
items.note: A common idiom for assessing the general impression or mood of a situation.

items.text: I'm just trying to get a read on
items.form: I'm just trying to get a read on
items.meaning: Used to explain that you are attempting to understand someone's intentions or a situation's dynamics.
items.example: I'm just trying to get a read on how the new manager prefers things to be done.
items.plain: I'm trying to understand how the new manager prefers things to be done.
items.note: A common idiom for assessing a person's mood, intentions, or a situation.

items.text: I'm just trying to figure out
items.form: I'm just trying to figure out
items.meaning: Used to explain that you are attempting to solve a problem or understand a situation.
items.example: I'm just trying to figure out the best route to the city centre from here.
items.plain: I'm trying to find the best route to the city centre from here.
items.note: A common, versatile phrase for problem-solving or understanding.

items.meaning: Used to explain that you are attempting to comprehend information or a situation.
items.example: I'm just trying to understand the implications of the new policy.
items.plain: I'm trying to comprehend the implications of the new policy.
items.note: A direct and polite way to ask for clarification or more information.

items.meaning: Used to explain that you are attempting to make something clearer or more precise.
items.example: I'm just trying to clarify the exact requirements for the submission.
items.plain: I'm trying to make the exact requirements for the submission clearer.
items.note: A professional and polite way to seek precision in communication.

items.meaning: Used to explain that you are attempting to verify information or an arrangement.
items.example: I'm just trying to confirm our meeting time for tomorrow.
items.plain: I'm trying to verify our meeting time for tomorrow.
items.note: A professional and polite way to ensure accuracy.

items.meaning: Used to explain that you are attempting to determine or prove a fact or situation.
items.example: I'm just trying to establish the root cause of the technical issue.
items.plain: I'm trying to determine the root cause of the technical issue.
items.note: A more formal way to express the goal of finding out something definite.

items.meaning: Used to explain that you are attempting to find out or confirm information precisely.
items.example: I'm just trying to ascertain the exact number of attendees.
items.plain: I'm trying to find out the exact number of attendees.
items.note: A more formal synonym for 'find out,' often used in professional contexts.

items.meaning: Used to explain that you are attempting to decide or conclude something after investigation.
items.example: I'm just trying to determine the best course of action.
items.plain: I'm trying to decide the best course of action.
items.note: A formal way to express the process of making a decision based on facts.

items.meaning: Used to explain that you are attempting to check the truth or accuracy of something.
items.example: I'm just trying to verify the figures in the report.
items.plain: I'm trying to check the figures in the report for accuracy.
items.note: A professional and polite way to ensure information is correct.

items.text: I'm just trying to see if
items.form: I'm just trying to see if
items.meaning: Used to explain that you are exploring a possibility or checking for an outcome.
items.example: I'm just trying to see if we can find a mutually convenient time.
items.plain: I'm trying to find out if we can find a mutually convenient time.
items.note: A casual and open-ended way to explore options or possibilities.

items.text: I'm just trying to work out
items.form: I'm just trying to work out
items.meaning: Used to explain that you are attempting to solve a problem or understand a complex situation.
items.example: I'm just trying to work out how all these pieces fit together.
items.plain: I'm trying to understand how all these pieces fit together.
items.note: A common, slightly informal idiom for problem-solving or comprehension.

items.text: I'm just trying to piece together
items.form: I'm just trying to piece together
items.meaning: Used to explain that you are attempting to understand a situation by combining various bits of information.
items.example: I'm just trying to piece together what happened during the outage.
items.plain: I'm trying to understand what happened during the outage by combining information.
items.note: A common idiom for reconstructing events from fragments of information.

items.text: I'm just trying to get a clearer picture
items.form: I'm just trying to get a clearer picture
items.meaning: Used to explain that you are attempting to gain a better understanding of a situation.
items.example: I'm just trying to get a clearer picture of the project's overall scope.
items.plain: I'm trying to understand the project's overall scope better.
items.note: A common idiom for seeking improved understanding or more details.

items.meaning: A polite and common way to signal that you are about to leave a conversation or place.
items.example: Well, I should get going; I have another meeting across town.
items.plain: I need to leave now; I have another meeting across town.
items.note: A very common and natural way to end a conversation gracefully.

items.text: It was lovely talking to you
items.form: It was lovely talking to you
items.meaning: A polite and warm way to express enjoyment of a conversation when parting.
items.example: It was lovely talking to you about your travels; perhaps we'll chat again soon.
items.plain: I enjoyed talking to you about your travels; perhaps we'll chat again soon.
items.note: A standard, friendly closing, suitable for both casual and professional settings.

items.text: I'll let you get back to it
items.form: I'll let you get back to it
items.meaning: A polite way to end a conversation, implying the other person has other tasks to attend to.
items.example: I'll let you get back to it; I know you have a busy afternoon ahead.
items.plain: I'll let you return to your work; I know you have a busy afternoon ahead.
items.note: Shows consideration and respect for the other person's time.

items.text: It was a pleasure meeting you
items.form: It was a pleasure meeting you
items.meaning: A formal and polite expression used when parting from someone you've just met.
items.example: It was a pleasure meeting you, Mr. Davies; I hope our paths cross again.
items.plain: I enjoyed meeting you, Mr. Davies; I hope our paths cross again.
items.note: Standard and appropriate for first encounters, especially in professional contexts.

items.meaning: A polite way to end a conversation, suggesting you are aware of the other person's time.
items.example: I mustn't keep you any longer; I know you have a tight schedule.
items.plain: I shouldn't hold you up any longer; I know you have a tight schedule.
items.note: A slightly more formal and very polite way to signal the end of a chat.

items.meaning: A casual and friendly way to say goodbye, implying you expect to encounter them again.
items.example: It was good catching up; I'll see you around the office next week.
items.plain: It was good catching up; I'll see you at the office next week.
items.note: Informal and friendly, suitable for colleagues or acquaintances you see regularly.

items.text: I'm afraid I have to run
items.form: I'm afraid I have to run
items.meaning: A polite and slightly apologetic way to state that you need to leave quickly.
items.example: I'm afraid I have to run; I'm already late for my next appointment.
items.plain: I need to leave quickly; I'm already late for my next appointment.
items.note: Common and natural, often used when you're in a hurry.

items.meaning: A concise and polite way to express enjoyment of an interaction or meeting.
items.example: Thank you for your insights; it's been a pleasure discussing this with you.
items.plain: Thank you for your insights; I enjoyed discussing this with you.
items.note: A versatile and elegant closing, suitable for various situations.

items.meaning: A common way to say goodbye, indicating you will contact them again soon.
items.example: Thanks for the information; I'll be in touch next week about the proposal.
items.plain: Thanks for the information; I will contact you next week about the proposal.
items.note: Standard and professional, implying future communication.

items.meaning: A friendly and polite request for someone to maintain contact with you.
items.example: It was great seeing you after so long; do keep in touch!
items.plain: It was great seeing you after so long; please stay in contact!
items.note: A warm and personal way to express a desire for continued connection.

items.text: It was good to see you
items.form: It was good to see you
items.meaning: A common and friendly way to express pleasure at having met or seen someone.
items.example: It was good to see you at the event; I hope you had a productive day.
items.plain: I was happy to see you at the event; I hope you had a productive day.
items.note: A standard, warm closing, especially for people you already know.

items.meaning: A polite way to end a conversation, indicating you are allowing the other person to continue their activity.
items.example: I'll leave you to it; I can see you're busy with those reports.
items.plain: I'll let you continue your work; I can see you're busy with those reports.
items.note: Shows consideration and respect for the other person's tasks.

items.meaning: A casual and friendly way to express appreciation for a conversation.
items.example: Well, thanks for the chat; I learned a lot about your new project.
items.plain: Well, thank you for the conversation; I learned a lot about your new project.
items.note: Informal and warm, suitable for casual conversations.

items.meaning: A sincere and polite way to express genuine pleasure from a discussion.
items.example: I've really enjoyed our conversation about sustainable living; it's given me much to think about.
items.plain: I genuinely liked talking to you about sustainable living; it's given me much to think about.
items.note: A warm and appreciative closing, suitable for engaging discussions.

items.meaning: A polite way to end a conversation, allowing the other person to continue with their activities.
items.example: I'll let you get on with your work now; I know you have a deadline.
items.plain: I'll let you continue with your work now; I know you have a deadline.
items.note: A common, understated British English phrase, similar to 'I'll let you get back to it'.

items.meaning: A slightly more emphatic and sincere version of 'It's been a pleasure'.
items.example: Thank you for inviting me; it's been a real pleasure attending your event.
items.plain: Thank you for inviting me; I truly enjoyed attending your event.
items.note: Conveys stronger appreciation and enjoyment than the simpler version.

items.text: I'll look forward to seeing you again
items.form: I'll look forward to seeing you again
items.meaning: A polite and hopeful way to express anticipation of a future meeting.
items.example: I'll look forward to seeing you again at the next industry conference.
items.plain: I hope to see you again at the next industry conference.
items.note: A standard, polite closing that suggests future interaction.

items.meaning: A friendly and common way to express enjoyment of updating each other on recent events.
items.example: It was great catching up with you after all this time; let's not leave it so long.
items.plain: It was good to hear your news after all this time; let's not leave it so long.
items.note: Informal and warm, suitable for friends or colleagues you haven't seen in a while.

items.meaning: A polite way to end a conversation, implying you are releasing the other person from the chat.
items.example: I'll let you go now; I know you have a busy schedule ahead.
items.plain: I'll end our conversation now; I know you have a busy schedule ahead.
items.note: A common and natural way to signal the end of a conversation, showing consideration.

items.meaning: A polite and professional way to thank someone for their valuable ideas or knowledge.
items.example: I appreciate your insights on the market trends; they've been very helpful.
items.plain: Thank you for your ideas on the market trends; they've been very helpful.
items.note: Formal and respectful, suitable for professional discussions.

items.meaning: A common, slightly informal way to express satisfaction at having briefly connected or communicated.
items.example: I'm glad we touched base before the meeting; it clarified a few things.
items.plain: I'm glad we spoke briefly before the meeting; it clarified a few things.
items.note: Often used in professional contexts for quick updates or checks.

items.meaning: A concise and professional way to describe a meeting or discussion that yielded good results.
items.example: Thank you for your time; it's been productive to discuss these matters.
items.plain: Thank you for your time; discussing these matters has been fruitful.
items.note: A professional and efficient way to conclude a work-related conversation.

items.meaning: A polite way to conclude an explanation or offer of assistance, wishing it to be useful.
items.example: So, that's how you submit the form. I hope that helps!
items.plain: So, that's how you submit the form. I hope it's useful!
items.note: A common and friendly closing when providing information or advice.

items.meaning: A polite offer to provide more detail or make something clearer if needed.
items.example: If anything is unclear, I'm happy to clarify further.
items.plain: If anything is unclear, I can explain it more.
items.note: Shows helpfulness and openness to further questions.

items.meaning: A professional and polite way to invite constructive criticism or opinions.
items.example: Please let me know your thoughts on the proposal; I'm always open to feedback.
items.plain: Please let me know your thoughts on the proposal; I welcome constructive criticism.
items.note: Conveys a receptive and collaborative attitude.

items.meaning: A common and enthusiastic way to express anticipation for a future event or meeting.
items.example: Our team lunch next week sounds great; I'm looking forward to it!
items.plain: Our team lunch next week sounds great; I'm excited about it!
items.note: A warm and positive expression of anticipation.

items.text: It's been a pleasure working with you
items.form: It's been a pleasure working with you
items.meaning: A polite and professional way to express enjoyment of a collaborative effort.
items.example: As the project concludes, it's been a pleasure working with you all.
items.plain: As the project concludes, I enjoyed working with you all.
items.note: Standard closing for professional collaborations, especially at project end.

items.text: I'll be sure to follow up
items.form: I'll be sure to follow up
items.meaning: A professional way to promise further action or communication regarding a topic.
items.example: Thanks for the information; I'll be sure to follow up with the team.
items.plain: Thanks for the information; I will definitely contact the team about it.
items.note: Conveys reliability and commitment to action.

items.meaning: A polite and common way to offer assistance or express willingness to do so.
items.example: If you need anything else, I'm happy to help.
items.plain: If you need anything else, I will gladly assist you.
items.note: A friendly and straightforward offer of support.

items.meaning: A friendly and slightly informal way to express satisfaction at having met or established contact.
items.example: I'm glad we connected at the networking event; it was very insightful.
items.plain: I'm happy we met at the networking event; it was very insightful.
items.note: Common in professional networking or social settings.

items.meaning: A common, slightly informal way to explain that you are making brief contact to check in or update.
items.example: I'm just touching base to see how the project is progressing.
items.plain: I'm just making brief contact to see how the project is progressing.
items.note: Often used in professional contexts for quick, informal check-ins.

items.meaning: A common, slightly informal way to explain that you are making contact to see how things are going.
items.example: I'm just checking in to see if you received my email.
items.plain: I'm just contacting you to see if you received my email.
items.note: A friendly and casual way to initiate contact or follow up.

items.meaning: A common, slightly informal way to explain that you are making contact to continue a previous discussion or action.
items.example: I'm just following up on our conversation from yesterday.
items.plain: I'm just continuing our conversation from yesterday.
items.note: A professional and efficient way to resume a previous interaction.

items.meaning: A common, slightly informal way to explain that you are making contact, often for the first time or after a break.
items.example: I'm just reaching out to introduce myself and offer my assistance.
items.plain: I'm just contacting you to introduce myself and offer my assistance.
items.note: A modern and friendly way to initiate communication, especially in professional settings.

items.text: I'm just dropping you a line
items.form: I'm just dropping you a line
items.meaning: A casual and friendly way to explain that you are sending a brief message.
items.example: I'm just dropping you a line to say hello and see how you're doing.
items.plain: I'm just sending you a quick message to say hello and see how you're doing.
items.note: More common in written communication (email/text) but can be used verbally to refer to it.

items.text: I'm just giving you a heads-up
items.form: I'm just giving you a heads-up
items.meaning: A common, slightly informal way to explain that you are providing advance notice or a warning.
items.example: I'm just giving you a heads-up that the meeting time has changed.
items.plain: I'm just informing you in advance that the meeting time has changed.
items.note: A friendly and efficient way to share important, time-sensitive information.

items.meaning: A common and straightforward way to explain that you are providing information.
items.example: I'm just letting you know that I'll be out of the office tomorrow.
items.plain: I'm just informing you that I'll be out of the office tomorrow.
items.note: A simple and direct way to convey information without formality.

items.meaning: A gentle way to introduce a question or express curiosity about a topic.
items.example: I'm just wondering about the logistics for the upcoming event.
items.plain: I'm curious about the logistics for the upcoming event.
items.note: Softens the inquiry, making it less direct and more conversational.

items.meaning: A polite and engaging way to express interest in learning more about a specific topic.
items.example: I'm just curious about your experience working abroad.
items.plain: I'd like to know more about your experience working abroad.
items.note: Shows genuine interest and encourages the other person to share details.

items.text: I'm just trying to confirm details
items.form: I'm just trying to confirm details
items.meaning: Used to explain that you are attempting to verify specific pieces of information.
items.example: I'm just trying to confirm details for the travel arrangements.
items.plain: I'm trying to verify specific pieces of information for the travel arrangements.
items.note: A professional and polite way to ensure accuracy in planning.

items.text: I'm just trying to get organized
items.form: I'm just trying to get organized
items.meaning: Used to explain that you are attempting to arrange your tasks or thoughts systematically.
items.example: With all these new projects, I'm just trying to get organized.
items.plain: With all these new projects, I'm trying to arrange my tasks systematically.
items.note: A common, relatable phrase for managing workload or information.

items.meaning: Used to explain that you are attempting to decide which tasks or issues are most important.
items.example: I'm just trying to prioritize my tasks for the week.
items.plain: I'm trying to decide which tasks are most important for the week.
items.note: A common, professional phrase for managing workload effectively.

items.text: I'm just trying to plan ahead
items.form: I'm just trying to plan ahead
items.meaning: Used to explain that you are attempting to make arrangements for the future.
items.example: I'm just trying to plan ahead for the upcoming holiday season.
items.plain: I'm trying to make arrangements for the upcoming holiday season.
items.note: A common, practical phrase for future preparation.

items.meaning: Used to explain that you are attempting to organize different elements or people to work together.
items.example: I'm just trying to coordinate schedules for the team meeting.
items.plain: I'm trying to organize schedules for the team meeting.
items.note: A common, professional phrase for managing logistics and teamwork.

items.meaning: A polite way to comment on good weather, often when doing an outdoor activity.
items.example: Lovely weather for it, isn't it? Perfect for a stroll in the park.
items.plain: The weather is nice, isn't it? It's perfect for a stroll in the park.
items.note: Common British English opener, often used when both parties are experiencing the same weather.

items.meaning: A general, polite inquiry about someone's well-being or current situation.
items.example: We haven't spoken in a while, how are things with you these days?
items.plain: We haven't spoken in a while, how are you doing these days?
items.note: A slightly more formal or considered alternative to "How are you?".

items.meaning: A polite way to initiate an introduction when you're unsure if you've been introduced before.
items.example: I don't believe we've met, I'm Sarah from the marketing department.
items.plain: I think we haven't met before, I'm Sarah from the marketing department.
items.note: Formal and polite, suitable for professional or semi-formal settings.

items.meaning: A polite way to ask permission to sit or stand with someone.
items.example: The cafe is quite full, mind if I join you at this table?
items.plain: The cafe is quite full, can I sit with you at this table?
items.note: Casual but polite, good for social situations like a coffee break or networking event.

items.meaning: Asking for someone's opinion or impression on a specific topic or situation.
items.example: What do you make of the new office layout? It's certainly different.
items.plain: What do you think about the new office layout? It's certainly different.
items.note: Invites a more considered opinion than a simple "do you like it?".

items.meaning: Acknowledging that someone has made a valid or insightful observation.
items.example: You're right, the traffic is terrible today. That's a good point about leaving earlier.
items.plain: You're right, the traffic is terrible today. You made a good observation about leaving earlier.
items.note: Simple, common, and effective for showing engagement and agreement.

items.meaning: Expressing that a new idea or perspective has been introduced to you.
items.example: I hadn't considered that, but it makes a lot of sense in this context.
items.plain: I didn't think of that before, but it makes a lot of sense in this context.
items.note: Polite way to acknowledge new information or a different viewpoint.

items.meaning: Introducing a frank or direct statement, often a personal opinion or admission.
items.example: To be honest with you, I'm finding the new project quite challenging.
items.plain: Frankly, I'm finding the new project quite challenging.
items.note: Common conversational filler, adds emphasis to sincerity.

items.meaning: Introducing a personal opinion, often one that might be slightly critical or strong.
items.example: If you ask me, they should have consulted us before making that decision.
items.plain: In my opinion, they should have consulted us before making that decision.
items.note: Can sound a little informal or opinionated, use with care in formal settings.

items.meaning: Expressing polite disagreement or uncertainty about a statement.
items.example: I'm not sure about that, I thought the deadline was next week.
items.plain: I don't know if that's correct, I thought the deadline was next week.
items.note: A soft way to express doubt or gentle disagreement without being confrontational.

items.meaning: Emphatically agreeing with someone's statement or observation.
items.example: "It's been a long week." "That's very true, I'm looking forward to the weekend."
items.plain: "It's been a long week." "That is absolutely correct, I'm looking forward to the weekend."
items.note: A common and natural way to show strong agreement.

items.meaning: Expressing complete agreement with what someone has said.
items.example: I couldn't agree more, the new policy is definitely a step in the right direction.
items.plain: I completely agree, the new policy is definitely a step in the right direction.
items.note: A strong but polite expression of agreement.

items.meaning: Acknowledging the validity of someone's argument, even if you don't fully agree.
items.example: That's a fair point about the budget constraints, we need to be realistic.
items.plain: You're right about the budget constraints, we need to be realistic.
items.note: Shows you're listening and considering their perspective.

items.meaning: Understanding someone's perspective or argument, without necessarily agreeing.
items.example: I see your point about the challenges, but I still think we should try.
items.plain: I understand your argument about the challenges, but I still think we should try.
items.note: Useful for acknowledging understanding in a polite disagreement.

items.meaning: Expressing uncertainty or reluctance to give a definitive answer.
items.example: "Will the project be finished on time?" "It's hard to say at this stage."
items.plain: "Will the project be finished on time?" "It's difficult to know for sure at this stage."
items.note: A common hedge, indicating a lack of clear information or a complex situation.

items.meaning: Expressing polite skepticism or partial disagreement.
items.example: I'm not entirely convinced that this approach will solve all our problems.
items.plain: I'm not completely sure that this approach will solve all our problems.
items.note: A softer way to express doubt than outright disagreement.

items.meaning: Indicating that you are verbalizing thoughts as they occur, not necessarily fully formed ideas.
items.example: I'm just thinking aloud here, but perhaps we could try a different strategy.
items.plain: I'm just saying what I'm thinking, but perhaps we could try a different strategy.
items.note: Useful for brainstorming or exploring ideas without committing to them.

items.meaning: A polite way to acknowledge an idea, often when you need time to process it or don't fully agree.
items.example: That's an interesting thought, I'll have to give it some more consideration.
items.plain: That's an interesting idea, I'll have to think about it more.
items.note: Can be a genuine compliment or a polite deferral.

items.text: I'm glad you brought that up
items.form: I'm glad you brought that up
items.meaning: Expressing appreciation that someone has raised a particular topic or issue.
items.example: I'm glad you brought that up, as I had a similar question about the schedule.
items.plain: I'm happy you mentioned that, as I had a similar question about the schedule.
items.note: Shows engagement and indicates the topic is relevant or important.

items.meaning: Asking to resume a conversation after an interruption or digression.
items.example: Sorry, my phone rang. Where were we before I was interrupted?
items.plain: Sorry, my phone rang. What were we talking about before I was interrupted?
items.note: Common and natural way to get back on track in a conversation.

items.meaning: Indicating that the information you're providing is based on your current knowledge, which might be incomplete.
items.example: As far as I know, the meeting is still scheduled for Tuesday morning.
items.plain: To my knowledge, the meeting is still scheduled for Tuesday morning.
items.note: A common hedge to qualify information and avoid absolute statements.

items.meaning: Inviting correction if your statement is inaccurate, showing openness to being corrected.
items.example: Correct me if I'm wrong, but didn't we discuss this last week?
items.plain: Please tell me if I'm mistaken, but didn't we discuss this last week?
items.note: Polite and collaborative, good for clarifying facts.

items.meaning: Indicating that something is generally true, with minor exceptions.
items.example: For the most part, the new system has been working quite smoothly.
items.plain: Generally, the new system has been working quite smoothly.
items.note: A useful qualifier to avoid overgeneralization.

items.meaning: Introducing a concise summary of a longer explanation.
items.example: In a nutshell, we need to cut costs and increase efficiency.
items.plain: To summarize briefly, we need to cut costs and increase efficiency.
items.note: Informal but widely understood, good for getting to the main point quickly.

items.text: To cut a long story short
items.form: To cut a long story short
items.meaning: Indicating that you are about to provide a brief summary of a longer narrative.
items.example: To cut a long story short, we ended up missing our flight.
items.plain: Briefly, we ended up missing our flight.
items.note: Common in informal storytelling, signals you're getting to the point.

items.meaning: Introducing a new, often related, topic or piece of information.
items.example: By the way, have you heard about the new cafe opening downtown?
items.plain: Incidentally, have you heard about the new cafe opening downtown?
items.note: Very common conversational transition, signals a slight shift in topic.

items.meaning: Introducing a related topic that was just mentioned or implied.
items.example: We were talking about travel, speaking of which, I'm planning a trip to Italy.
items.plain: We were talking about travel, and that reminds me, I'm planning a trip to Italy.
items.note: Smooth transition, linking the current topic to a new, related one.

items.meaning: Used to transition to a new topic or to conclude a discussion, often related to the previous point.
items.example: We've covered a lot of ground today. On that note, I think we should wrap up.
items.plain: We've covered a lot of ground today. Considering that, I think we should wrap up.
items.note: Can be used to smoothly end a conversation or shift focus.

items.meaning: Introducing a question that you are asking purely for interest, not for any specific purpose.
items.example: Just out of curiosity, how long have you been working here?
items.plain: I'm simply curious, how long have you been working here?
items.note: Softens a direct question, making it sound less intrusive.

items.meaning: A polite way to introduce a comment or opinion, often one that might be slightly bold or critical.
items.example: If I may say so, your presentation was exceptionally well-prepared.
items.plain: Your presentation was exceptionally well-prepared, in my opinion.
items.note: Adds a touch of formality and politeness, often used for compliments or gentle suggestions.

items.meaning: Indicating that you have inferred something from what you've heard or observed.
items.example: I gather that you've been quite busy with the new project lately.
items.plain: I understand from what I've heard that you've been quite busy with the new project lately.
items.note: Polite way to show you've been paying attention and making connections.

items.meaning: Introducing a personal opinion or observation in a softened, less assertive way.
items.example: It seems to me that we're making good progress on this task.
items.plain: I think that we're making good progress on this task.
items.note: A common hedge, making a statement sound less like a definitive fact.

items.meaning: Expressing a reasonable assumption or expectation about a situation.
items.example: I'd imagine that working from home has its own set of challenges.
items.plain: I would assume that working from home has its own set of challenges.
items.note: Polite way to show empathy or understanding by making an educated guess.

items.meaning: Indicating that you have received information, often indirectly or from a reliable source.
items.example: I'm given to understand that the new policy will be implemented next month.
items.plain: I have been informed that the new policy will be implemented next month.
items.note: Formal and slightly indirect, good for conveying information without stating a source.

items.meaning: Introducing a statement that you believe to be true, but are open to correction.
items.example: If I'm not mistaken, you mentioned you were moving to a new apartment soon?
items.plain: I think I'm right, you mentioned you were moving to a new apartment soon?
items.note: Polite way to check information or recall without sounding demanding.

items.meaning: Indicating that you were on the verge of doing or saying something.
items.example: I was just about to ask you the same question about the project.
items.plain: I was going to ask you the same question about the project.
items.note: Common for showing shared thoughts or intentions.

items.meaning: A polite and informal way to express that you would like something.
items.example: It's been a long day, I wouldn't say no to a cup of tea.
items.plain: It's been a long day, I would like a cup of tea.
items.note: Casual and friendly, often used for food, drink, or a break.

items.meaning: Expressing willingness to do what someone has asked or requested.
items.example: If you need me to send those documents, I'm happy to oblige.
items.plain: If you need me to send those documents, I will gladly do so.
items.note: Slightly more formal than "happy to help", implies fulfilling a request.

items.meaning: A polite and regretful way to say no or to confirm something negative.
items.example: "Do you have any more of those reports?" "I'm afraid not, we've run out."
items.plain: "Do you have any more of those reports?" "No, we've run out."
items.note: Softer than a direct "no", shows regret.

items.meaning: A polite and regretful way to confirm something negative or undesirable.
items.example: "Is the meeting still on for Friday?" "I'm afraid so, despite the short notice."
items.plain: "Is the meeting still on for Friday?" "Yes, unfortunately, despite the short notice."
items.note: Softer than a direct "yes" when the news is unwelcome.

items.meaning: Stating that something is so obvious it doesn't need to be said, but you're saying it anyway.
items.example: It goes without saying that we appreciate your hard work on this project.
items.plain: It's obvious that we appreciate your hard work on this project.
items.note: Emphasizes the obviousness or importance of a statement.

items.meaning: Checking for understanding or agreement, often when expressing something difficult to articulate.
items.example: It's just a bit overwhelming sometimes, all the new responsibilities, you know what I mean?
items.plain: It's just a bit overwhelming sometimes, all the new responsibilities, do you understand?
items.note: Informal conversational tag, seeks empathy or confirmation.

items.meaning: Asking if someone understands an indirect or implied meaning.
items.example: We need to be more "efficient" with our resources, if you catch my drift.
items.plain: We need to be more "efficient" with our resources, do you understand what I'm implying?
items.note: Informal, often used when hinting at something or being subtly critical.

items.meaning: Introducing a very direct and honest statement, often one that might be uncomfortable.
items.example: To be perfectly frank, I don't think this proposal is viable in its current form.
items.plain: Honestly, I don't think this proposal is viable in its current form.
items.note: Stronger and more formal than "to be honest", signals directness.

items.meaning: Introducing a confession or an acknowledgment, often of something slightly surprising or reluctant.
items.example: I must admit, I was a bit skeptical at first, but the results are impressive.
items.plain: I have to confess, I was a bit skeptical at first, but the results are impressive.
items.note: Adds a personal touch, showing a shift in perspective or a candid thought.

items.meaning: Introducing a very honest statement, often one that might be surprising or slightly negative.
items.example: I'm not going to lie, that presentation was a bit dull.
items.plain: Honestly, that presentation was a bit dull.
items.note: Informal and direct, emphasizes sincerity.

items.meaning: Acknowledging that someone's statement is true, often with a hint of understatement or irony.
items.example: "It's been a challenging week." "You could say that, I've barely slept."
items.plain: "It's been a challenging week." "Yes, it has been very challenging, I've barely slept."
items.note: Often used to agree with an understatement, implying the situation is worse.

items.meaning: Expressing that a particular outcome or situation is expected or plausible.
items.example: I wouldn't be surprised if they announced a new policy next quarter.
items.plain: I would expect them to announce a new policy next quarter.
items.note: Indicates a strong likelihood or a feeling of inevitability.

items.meaning: Used to redirect the conversation to a previous topic after a digression.
items.example: To get back to what we were discussing, how will this impact our team?
items.plain: Let's return to what we were discussing, how will this impact our team?
items.note: Polite way to steer the conversation back on track.

items.meaning: Used to resume a statement or explanation after an interruption.
items.example: As I was saying, the new software update will require some training.
items.plain: To continue what I was saying, the new software update will require some training.
items.note: Common after a brief interruption, signals continuation.

items.meaning: Acknowledging the validity of someone's argument or observation.
items.example: You've got a point about the timing; it might be better to wait.
items.plain: You are right about the timing; it might be better to wait.
items.note: Informal and common way to concede a point.

items.meaning: Explaining that you are attempting to express a thought or idea clearly.
items.example: I'm just trying to articulate my concerns about the project timeline.
items.plain: I'm attempting to express my concerns about the project timeline clearly.
items.note: Used when formulating complex thoughts, signals a process of expression.

items.meaning: Politely indicating that you are having difficulty understanding the current point.
items.example: I'm not quite following your logic on that last point, could you elaborate?
items.plain: I don't fully understand your logic on that last point, could you elaborate?
items.note: A polite way to ask for clarification without sounding critical.

items.meaning: Stating that something is an accepted fact or a foregone conclusion.
items.example: That's a given; we always prioritize client satisfaction above all else.
items.plain: That is an accepted fact; we always prioritize client satisfaction above all else.
items.note: Informal but common, implies something is universally understood.

items.meaning: Introducing a statement that you believe to be true and unlikely to be disputed.
items.example: It's safe to say that everyone enjoyed the team-building event.
items.plain: We can confidently say that everyone enjoyed the team-building event.
items.note: A common way to express a widely accepted conclusion or observation.

items.text: I'm just trying to be helpful
items.form: I'm just trying to be helpful
items.meaning: Explaining that your intention is to assist, often when offering unsolicited advice or information.
items.example: I'm just trying to be helpful by suggesting an alternative approach.
items.plain: My intention is to help by suggesting an alternative approach.
items.note: Can soften advice, but sometimes used defensively.

items.text: I'm just trying to be polite
items.form: I'm just trying to be polite
items.meaning: Explaining that your actions or words are motivated by good manners.
items.example: I'm just trying to be polite by offering you the last piece of cake.
items.plain: I'm simply trying to show good manners by offering you the last piece of cake.
items.note: Used to explain a gesture or remark, sometimes with a hint of irony.

items.meaning: A polite way to end a conversation, implying you don't want to take up more of their time.
items.example: Well, I won't keep you, I know you have a busy afternoon ahead.
items.plain: I don't want to take up any more of your time, I know you have a busy afternoon ahead.
items.note: Polite and considerate way to signal the end of a chat.

items.meaning: Expressing that an experience or conversation was particularly enjoyable or special.
items.example: Meeting you and hearing your stories, it's been a real treat.
items.plain: Meeting you and hearing your stories has been very enjoyable.
items.note: More emphatic and personal than "a pleasure", often used for a memorable interaction.

items.meaning: An informal way to say goodbye, implying you expect to see them again soon.
items.example: Right, I need to head off now, I'll catch you later.
items.plain: Okay, I need to leave now, I'll see you again soon.
items.note: Casual and friendly, suitable for colleagues or acquaintances you see regularly.

items.meaning: A friendly and slightly informal way to say goodbye, wishing someone well.
items.example: It was good to chat, take care now!
items.plain: It was good to chat, goodbye and be well!
items.note: Common in British English, friendly and warm.

items.meaning: A common and friendly way to say goodbye, wishing someone good fortune.
items.example: I'm off to my next meeting, all the best with your presentation!
items.plain: I'm off to my next meeting, I wish you good luck with your presentation!
items.note: Versatile and widely used for ending conversations or emails.

items.meaning: A polite and slightly formal way to say you need to leave quickly.
items.example: I'm afraid I must dash, I have another appointment in five minutes.
items.plain: I'm sorry, I have to leave quickly, I have another appointment in five minutes.
items.note: More formal than "I have to run", implies a sudden need to depart.

items.meaning: Expressing that the conversation was productive and yielded good results or insights.
items.example: Thank you for your time, it's been a fruitful discussion.
items.plain: Thank you for your time, this discussion has been very productive.
items.note: Formal and positive, suitable for professional or academic settings.

items.meaning: An informal way to say goodbye, implying you expect to meet again.
items.example: Right, I'm heading out. I'll be seeing you around the office.
items.plain: Okay, I'm leaving. I'll see you again around the office.
items.note: Casual and friendly, common among colleagues or neighbors.

items.meaning: A polite and friendly way to say goodbye, anticipating a future meeting.
items.example: Well, it's been great catching up. Until next time!
items.plain: Well, it's been great catching up. Goodbye until we meet again!
items.note: Versatile, can be used in both formal and informal contexts.

items.text: I very much look forward to
items.form: I very much look forward to
items.meaning: Expressing strong anticipation and eagerness for a future event or interaction.
items.example: I very much look forward to our next meeting to discuss this further.
items.plain: I am very eager for our next meeting to discuss this further.
items.note: More formal and emphatic than "I'm looking forward to it".

items.meaning: Politely expressing reservations or unease about a situation or proposal.
items.example: I'm not entirely comfortable with the proposed changes to the project scope.
items.plain: I have some reservations about the proposed changes to the project scope.
items.note: A soft but clear way to express disagreement or concern.

items.text: I'm not at liberty to say
items.form: I'm not at liberty to say
items.meaning: Politely declining to provide information because you are not authorized to do so.
items.example: I'm not at liberty to say who will be taking over the department.
items.plain: I am not allowed to say who will be taking over the department.
items.note: Formal and professional, used when information is confidential.

items.meaning: Introducing a complaint or criticism by first stating that you don't usually complain.
items.example: I'm not one to complain, but the air conditioning in here is quite strong.
items.plain: I don't usually complain, but the air conditioning in here is quite strong.
items.note: Softens a complaint, making it sound more reasonable or exceptional.

items.meaning: Introducing a piece of information that might be considered gossip, while disclaiming the act of gossiping.
items.example: I'm not one to gossip, but I heard they're reorganizing the team.
items.plain: I don't usually spread rumors, but I heard they're reorganizing the team.
items.note: A common conversational hedge before sharing potentially sensitive information.

items.meaning: Introducing a comment about someone's actions or choices, while disclaiming any moral judgment.
items.example: I'm not one to judge, but that decision seems a bit risky.
items.plain: I don't usually criticize others, but that decision seems a bit risky.
items.note: Used to offer an opinion without appearing judgmental.

items.meaning: Introducing a statement about your own achievements or qualities, while disclaiming pride.
items.example: I'm not one to boast, but I did manage to finish the report ahead of schedule.
items.plain: I don't usually brag, but I did manage to finish the report ahead of schedule.
items.note: A humble way to share a personal success.

items.meaning: Introducing a question that might be considered personal, while assuring you don't intend to intrude.
items.example: I'm not one to pry, but how was your weekend trip?
items.plain: I don't usually ask personal questions, but how was your weekend trip?
items.note: Softens a potentially intrusive question.

items.meaning: Introducing a point of disagreement by stating that you generally avoid arguments.
items.example: I'm not one to argue, but I think there's a different way to look at this.
items.plain: I don't usually argue, but I think there's a different way to look at this.
items.note: A polite way to introduce a counter-argument.

items.text: I'm not one to rush things
items.form: I'm not one to rush things
items.meaning: Explaining that you prefer to take your time and not hurry.
items.example: I'm not one to rush things, so I'll take my time reviewing the proposal.
items.plain: I don't usually hurry, so I'll take my time reviewing the proposal.
items.note: Used to justify a slower pace or careful approach.

items.text: I'm not one to make a fuss
items.form: I'm not one to make a fuss
items.meaning: Explaining that you prefer to avoid causing trouble or drawing attention.
items.example: I'm not one to make a fuss, but this coffee is cold.
items.plain: I don't usually cause trouble, but this coffee is cold.
items.note: Used to soften a complaint or request, implying it's a rare occurrence.

i'll let you get back to it.note: Checker slip: The key accurately defines the expression as a polite conversational exit strategy.
